subject: Microbiology
subtopic: Sleeping sickness: Trypanosoma brucei gambiense/rhodesiense, tsetse transmission, stages, diagnosis and treatment
concept: Human African trypanosomiasis is a vector-borne protozoal disease caused by T. brucei gambiense or T. brucei rhodesiense and transmitted by infected tsetse flies.

content.definition: Human African trypanosomiasis is a vector-borne protozoal disease caused by T. brucei gambiense or T. brucei rhodesiense and transmitted by infected tsetse flies.
content.explanation: Trypanosomes multiply first in blood and lymph (haemolymphatic stage), then may cross the blood-brain barrier causing meningoencephalitic disease with sleep-cycle disturbance and neurologic manifestations.
content.mechanism: Trypanosomes multiply first in blood and lymph (haemolymphatic stage), then may cross the blood-brain barrier causing meningoencephalitic disease with sleep-cycle disturbance and neurologic manifestations.
content.structure: Clinically important organism-specific structural and biologic features are summarized in the explanation and terminology fields.
content.function: The pathogen's biologic properties determine transmission, tissue tropism, clinical manifestations and diagnostic strategy.
causes: Gambiense disease is mainly associated with human reservoirs
Rhodesiense disease has an important animal reservoir
effects: First stage: fever, headache, lymphadenopathy and pruritus
Second stage: behavioral change, confusion, coordination problems and sleep disturbance
content.clinical_relevance: This is an official Hematology microbiology syllabus organism/disease. Human African Trypanosomiasis should be interpreted using current diagnostic and treatment guidance.
content.diagnosis: Definitive diagnosis rests on microscopic detection of trypanosomes. Blood detection is particularly useful in rhodesiense disease; gambiense diagnosis is more difficult. CSF examination is used for staging.
content.treatment: Treatment depends on subspecies and stage and has changed with modern WHO/CDC guidance; specialist guidance is important because CNS-stage therapy differs from first-stage therapy.
